nameStory: The Long-tailed Duck gets its name from the male's dramatically elongated tail feathers that can stretch nearly as long as the rest of his body! These fancy tail plumes are most prominent during breeding season, creating an unmistakable silhouette as the duck swims or flies. It's like nature gave this sea duck a built-in streamer flag.
description: The Long-tailed Duck is a compact, hardy sea duck that's perfectly built for life on cold ocean waters. Males are particularly striking with their long, curved tail feathers and bold black-and-white plumage that changes dramatically between seasons. Females are more subdued in brown and white tones but share the same stocky, seafaring build. These medium-sized ducks are excellent divers, spending much of their time underwater hunting for food in coastal waters.

idTips.label: Male's long tail
idTips.description: Breeding males sport impossibly long, thin black tail feathers that curve gracefully behind them - you'll hear them whistling through the wind as the duck moves

idTips.label: Seasonal plumage change
idTips.description: Males dramatically switch from mostly white bodies with dark backs in winter to mostly dark bodies with white patches in summer - like wearing opposite jerseys

idTips.label: Diving behavior
idTips.description: Watch them disappear completely underwater for 30-60 seconds at a time, popping up unexpectedly elsewhere - they're like feathered submarines

idTips.label: Compact sea duck build
idTips.description: Stocky, round bodies that sit low in the water with relatively small heads - built like little tugboats for riding rough ocean swells

idTips.label: Vocal calls
idTips.description: Males make musical, yodeling calls that carry far across the water - a distinctive 'ow-ow-owdle-ow' that sounds almost human

habitat: Long-tailed Ducks prefer the cold, open waters off New England's rocky coastlines, especially around headlands, offshore islands, and areas with strong currents. You'll spot them from shore at places like Cape Ann in Massachusetts, the Maine coast near Acadia, or from ferry boats heading to offshore islands. They favor deeper waters where they can dive for shellfish and marine invertebrates, often gathering in loose flocks that bob and weave with the ocean swells.

seasonality.spring: Males begin showing their impressive breeding plumage and long tail feathers become most prominent. Listen for their musical calls increasing as they prepare for their journey to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Most have departed for Arctic tundra breeding areas, though a few non-breeding individuals may linger along the coast in darker summer plumage.
seasonality.fall: First returning birds appear in late fall, with males beginning to show their striking winter white plumage. Numbers build steadily through the season.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for viewing! Large flocks gather in coastal waters, with males sporting their most dramatic black-and-white winter plumage and fully developed tail streamers.

funFact: Long-tailed Ducks are among the deepest diving ducks in the world, regularly plunging down 200 feet below the ocean surface - deeper than a 20-story building is tall - to hunt for clams and other shellfish on the seafloor!
confusionNotes: Female Long-tailed Ducks can be confused with other brown sea ducks like female Common Goldeneyes or Buffleheads, but remember the memory trick: Long-tailed Ducks have longer necks and more pointed bills, plus they're usually farther offshore in rougher water where the 'long-distance swimmers' hang out.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly called the 'Oldsquaw' but the name was changed to Long-tailed Duck in 2000 to be more descriptive and less potentially offensive. In some field guides or older references, you might still see the former name, so don't be confused - they're the same bird!
compareHints: As the only member of its genus Clangula, the Long-tailed Duck is quite unique among New England ducks. Compared to other sea ducks like scoters or eiders, Long-tailed Ducks are smaller and more agile, with much more dramatic seasonal plumage changes. Unlike the bulkier diving ducks, they have a more streamlined build and those unmistakable elongated tail feathers on males that no other duck in our region can match.
